common_name: April Snow Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; April Snow is part of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy camellia breeding program at the U.S. National Arboretum, selected for reliable flowering and better winter hardiness than typical Camellia japonica.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and mulch well to protect shallow roots. April Snow is one of the cold-hardy camellia introductions from Dr. William Ackerman's breeding program at the U.S. National Arboretum, developed to extend reliable camellia flowering into colder parts of the Southeast and mid-Atlantic than standard Camellia japonica cultivars can tolerate. It produces medium, formal double white flowers in early spring on a dense, rounded evergreen shrub, with glossy dark green foliage that provides structure and screening year-round even when not in bloom. Feed lightly with an acid-forming azalea-camellia fertilizer after flowering and again in early summer, and avoid heavy pruning except to shape, since camellias set next year's flower buds on the current season's growth. In Gulf Coast gardens, afternoon shade helps protect the flowers and foliage from scorch during hot spells.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Survivor is a Camellia oleifera hybrid from Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy breeding program, among the most winter-hardy camellias available, tolerant of considerably colder conditions than standard Camellia japonica.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving some winter sun where possible to help harden off growth before hard freezes. Survivor is one of the toughest of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bred from Camellia oleifera crossed with Camellia japonica specifically to push reliable camellia flowering and foliage survival further north and into colder microclimates than the species alone can handle. It bears small to medium single white flowers in fall into early winter on a dense, twiggy, evergreen shrub, and its exceptional hardiness makes it a forgiving choice for gardeners at the colder edge of camellia country or in an exposed Gulf Coast site prone to occasional hard freezes. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom, keep the root zone mulched, and prune only lightly to shape immediately after flowering finishes.

common_name: Winter's Star Camellia (Cold-Hardy Orchid-Pink Ackerman Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Star is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias, bred for reliable fall-into-winter bloom and better cold tolerance than standard camellias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold snaps. Winter's Star belongs to the Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids developed at the U.S. National Arboretum, crossing Camellia oleifera into the hardier fall-blooming Camellia hiemalis lineage to combine dependable fall-into-winter flowering with markedly better cold tolerance than most camellias. It produces single, orchid-pink flowers with prominent golden stamens on a vigorous, spreading evergreen shrub, blooming over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in flower. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

common_name: Snow Flurry Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Snow Flurry is another of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy Winter-series camellia hybrids, grown for its abundant white anemone-form flowers and improved cold tolerance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with some protection from harsh winter wind in the coldest parts of its range. Snow Flurry is one of the most floriferous of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy Winter-series camellia hybrids, smothering its spreading, dense evergreen branches in small, white, anemone-form flowers with ruffled centers over a long fall-into-winter bloom season. Its Camellia oleifera parentage gives it notably better cold hardiness than standard Camellia japonica, letting gardeners at the colder edge of camellia range enjoy a heavy floral display that would otherwise be unreliable. The naturally spreading, slightly weeping habit also makes it useful for a low, wide evergreen groundcover-like planting rather than the more upright shape typical of most camellias. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune lightly only to shape.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Spider Web is a variegated Fatsia japonica cultivar with fine white speckling scattered across each large, glossy, deeply lobed leaf, giving the foliage a frosted, cobweb-like appearance.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, protected from direct hot afternoon sun, which scorches the fine variegation faster than it would plain green foliage. Spider Web is a striking variegated sport of the popular architectural shade shrub Fatsia japonica, with each large, glossy, hand-shaped leaf speckled in fine white flecks that give the whole plant a frosted, almost cobweb-dusted look distinct from the bolder white-edged variegation of other Fatsia cultivars. It brings dramatic tropical-looking texture to a deep shade bed where few other shrubs perform, and its bold foliage pairs well with ferns, hostas, and other fine-textured shade perennials as a contrasting anchor plant. Established plants tolerate the humid Gulf Coast summer well but appreciate protection from hard freezes in the colder parts of their range; a hard frost may damage foliage even where the roots survive and resprout in spring. Prune only to remove damaged or overly leggy stems, since Fatsia branches slowly and responds well to renewal pruning if it becomes overgrown.
